strengths: Sound and well-motivated problem formulation: Tackles zero-shot anomaly generation (ZSAG) in a completely training-free manner, directly addressing the paradox of few-shot generation methods that rely on scarce defect annotations.

Methodological coherence: The proposed framework smartly integrates several components tailored for anomaly synthesis—specifically, dual-branch delta-denoising attribution (contrasting normal and defective prompt trajectories), normal-reference partial noise initialization to preserve background consistency, and token-level prompt refinement with attention biasing to isolate defect semantics.

Solid empirical gains in downstream detection: Evaluated by training downstream inspection models, DeltaDeno consistently outperforms the primary zero-shot competitor (AnomalyAny) across both image- and pixel-level metrics (e.g., improving average AUCi from 77.6% to 84.7% and APp from 26.5% to 30.5% on MVTec AD).
Clear presentation and ablation analysis: The manuscript is well written, featuring well-structured diagrams, comprehensive visual defect comparisons, and informative component ablations.
weaknesses: Conceptual overlap with prior editing paradigms: The core mechanism of contrasting denoiser predictions under paired prompts to derive an edit mask closely mirrors DiffEdit (Couairon et al., 2022), while latent blending follows Blended Latent Diffusion / SDEdit. The paper would benefit from a clearer discussion explicitly contrasting DeltaDeno's formulation against DiffEdit.

Narrow benchmark diversity in the main paper: Quantitative comparisons (Tables 1, 2, and 3) are provided exclusively on MVTec AD. Given that generalization across diverse domains is the primary claim of ZSAG, including results on other standard benchmarks (e.g., VisA, KolektorSDD, or MPDD) in the main paper would significantly strengthen the empirical validation.

Limited downstream detector variety: Downstream utility is evaluated solely using a simple U-Net trained on 100 generated samples per category. Demonstrating whether the synthesized anomalies boost performance in modern zero-shot / few-shot anomaly detection pipelines (e.g., WinCLIP, AnomalyCLIP, or modern feature-reconstruction backbones) would provide stronger proof of practical utility.

Inference cost and hyperparameter sensitivity: Running two synchronized diffusion passes alongside SAM foreground segmentation and latent prompt refinement incurs non-trivial computational overhead. Reporting inference latency/throughput and analyzing the sensitivity to key thresholds (e.g., tau_mid, tau_final, beta, and gamma) would improve reproducibility and practical assessment.

strengths: Practical problem framing: Targeting zero-shot, training-free anomaly generation without requiring real defect samples or costly fine-tuning addresses a realistic bottleneck in visual anomaly inspection.

Well-designed technical pipeline: Combining synchronized dual-branch diffusion difference accumulation (delta-denoising attribution) with late-stage latent inpainting, normal-reference warm start, token refinement, and spatial attention biasing provides an effective formulation for localized anomaly synthesis.

Comprehensive validation against the primary zero-shot competitor: Outperforms AnomalyAny on downstream anomaly detection metrics (AUCi, APi, AUCp, APp) on MVTec AD, alongside solid qualitative ablations demonstrating the utility of each proposed module.
weaknesses: High conceptual overlap with DiffEdit: DiffEdit (Couairon et al., 2022) already proposed contrasting noise predictions between source and target text prompts under a shared schedule to derive a spatial edit mask for inpainting. The paper should explicitly contrast its delta-denoising attribution formulation against DiffEdit and justify why latent trajectory discrepancies $d_{t-1}(u)$ are superior to DiffEdit's noise prediction differences.

Undiscussed reliance on SAM: Step 1 of Algorithm 1 and Section 3.3 rely on an external foundation model (SAM) to generate the coarse foreground mask $M_{fg}$ for early-stage attention biasing. The ablation study does not isolate the impact or failure modes of this SAM-generated prior.

Evaluation scope and downstream detector variety: Downstream evaluation is confined to training a simple U-Net on synthetic defects from a single normal reference image per class on MVTec AD. Evaluating whether generated samples benefit standard anomaly detection frameworks or modern architectures (e.g., augmenting existing unsupervised baselines like PatchCore/SimpleNet) across additional benchmarks (e.g., VisA) would substantially strengthen the empirical claims.

Variability across defect types: As observed in Table 2, pixel-level AP (APp) remains quite low for complex or fine-grained categories (e.g., cable at 8.0%, capsule at 5.8%, screw at 4.7%), where it occasionally falls behind AnomalyAny, highlighting remaining limitations in fine-grained defect generation.

strengths: Tackles an important and practical problem in industrial vision: zero-shot anomaly generation (ZSAG) without requiring anomalous training samples or fine-tuning.
The overall framework is coherent, integrating synchronized dual-branch diffusion, delta attribution for dynamic masking, latent inpainting, and spatial attention biasing.
Empirical improvements over the main zero-shot baseline (AnomalyAny) in both generation diversity metrics and downstream anomaly classification/segmentation on MVTec AD using a U-Net detector.
Ablation studies isolate the relative contributions of latent inpainting, spatial attention biasing, and prompt refinement.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty relative to established diffusion editing techniques: The core mechanism of contrasting noise predictions across source and target prompts under a shared schedule to derive a spatial edit mask and subsequent inpainting is fundamentally identical to DiffEdit (Couairon et al., 2022). The manuscript adapts DiffEdit to normal/defect prompt pairs and adds heuristic regularizations, but does not sufficiently differentiate its technical attribution mechanism from DiffEdit.

Evaluation on downstream anomaly detection is restricted to a basic U-Net trained from scratch: Modern industrial anomaly detection relies on strong feature-based or foundation models (e.g., PatchCore, SimpleNet, WinCLIP, UniAD). The paper only evaluates a standalone U-Net trained exclusively on 100 synthetic defect images, leaving open whether the generated samples provide tangible value as data augmentation for competitive, state-of-the-art anomaly detectors.

Evaluation dataset scope is narrow in the main text: The quantitative evaluation is conducted solely on MVTec AD. Evaluating across more diverse and challenging benchmarks (such as VisA, MPDD, or Real-IAD) is necessary to substantiate claims of robust cross-category and cross-domain generalization.

Inappropriate use of Inception Score (IS) for industrial defect images: IS measures class conditional entropy based on ImageNet pretraining, which has well-documented deficiencies when applied to specialized, single-class texture and industrial object images.

Undisclosed dependency and implementation details regarding SAM: Algorithm 1 utilizes a foreground mask $M_{\text{fg}}$ from SAM (Segment Anything) to bias attention in early steps, yet details on how SAM is prompted (e.g., automatic mask generation, points, or text) and its contribution to the final mask quality are omitted.

Potential manual prompt engineering: Anomaly semantic distillation relies on manually curated descriptive anchors $e_{\text{detail}}$ (e.g., specifying morphological attributes). The extent of manual prompt tuning required per defect category is not analyzed, weakening the claim of fully automatic zero-shot generation.

strengths: Well-motivated setting: Zero-Shot Anomaly Generation (ZSAG) addresses the core paradox of few-shot anomaly generation, which relies on scarce real defects for fine-tuning. A training-free zero-shot approach is highly relevant and practical for industrial inspection.

Technically sound and cohesive formulation: Contrasting synchronized diffusion trajectories driven by minimal prompt pairs to derive delta-denoising attribution maps offers an effective, training-free way to obtain pixel-aligned defect masks without suffering from the low-resolution artifacts of raw cross-attention maps.

Well-designed complementary components: The combination of token-level prompt refinement (anchoring the anomaly token while regularizing context) and spatially-biased cross-attention (leveraging early foreground priors and refined mid-stage masks) effectively confines edits to plausible defect regions.

Strong experimental validation: Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations on MVTec AD and VisA demonstrate consistent improvements in both generation quality/diversity (IS, IC-LPIPS) and downstream detection metrics (AUC and AP) over prior ZSAG baselines (e.g., AnomalyAny, AnoStyler), and the framework easily scales to advanced backbones like FLUX.1-dev.

Thorough ablation and supplementary analysis: The paper and appendix provide comprehensive studies on the impact of each component, threshold sensitivities, runtime/memory efficiency, and the dependence on SAM.
weaknesses: Discussion of similarity to DiffEdit: Contrasting predictions between reference and target prompts to derive an edit mask shares conceptual similarity with DiffEdit (Couairon et al., 2022). While DiffEdit is cited in the related work, a more explicit comparison highlighting the exact technical differences in trajectory synchronization, latent accumulation, and anomaly-specific design would clarify the distinct contribution.

Sensitivity to hyperparameters and thresholding: The pipeline introduces multiple hyperparameters, notably the mid-stage threshold $\tau_{\text{mid}}$, the final mask threshold, prompt refinement learning rate $\eta$, and attention bias weight $\beta$. While the authors suggest a unified default configuration, the quantitative sensitivity in Table 6 indicates notable variations across thresholds.

Reliance on SAM for foreground prior: In the early denoising stage, cross-attention biasing relies on SAM to obtain foreground regions $M_{\text{fg}}$. Although Appendix C.2 evaluates an all-ones fallback showing acceptable performance, incorporating SAM adds complexity and dependency to the generation pipeline.

Downstream evaluation protocol limitations: Downstream performance is evaluated by training a basic U-Net from scratch on 100 synthesized samples. While this matches the protocol in AnomalyAny, assessing compatibility with established downstream anomaly detection baselines or testing on more complex real-world anomalies (e.g., logical/structural anomalies beyond texture/surface defects) would provide a more complete assessment.

strengths: The paper addresses a very practical and important setting: zero-shot anomaly generation (ZSAG) without requiring real defective training samples, model fine-tuning, or category-specific adaptation.

The core idea of delta-denoising attribution—synchronizing two diffusion branches conditioned on normal vs. anomaly prompts and accumulating per-step latent discrepancies to automatically derive localization masks—is technically sound, well-motivated, and elegant.

The combination of token-level prompt refinement, spatial cross-attention biasing, and late-stage latent inpainting effectively prevents off-target drift and yields sharp, photorealistic, and localized anomalies.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across standard benchmarks (MVTec AD and VisA) demonstrates consistent gains over prior ZSAG methods (AnomalyAny, AnoStyler) and competitive performance against few-shot methods in downstream detection.
The framework demonstrates strong model generality by seamlessly transferring from Stable Diffusion v1.5 to FLUX.1-dev with notable performance boosts.

The paper and appendix provide thorough ablations (dissecting prompt refinement, attention biasing, inpainting, threshold sensitivity, SAM dependence, and efficiency) as well as an insightful critique of existing evaluation protocols in ZSAG.
weaknesses: Downstream detection effectiveness is evaluated primarily using a single simple U-Net segmentation network; evaluating on diverse established industrial AD frameworks (e.g., feature-embedding or reconstruction-based detectors) would better confirm the general utility of the synthesized data.

The two-branch synchronized denoising process inherently doubles the forward pass operations during early diffusion stages compared to standard single-branch generation, although runtime remains manageable relative to heavier baselines.

The method requires two threshold hyperparameters (early-stage mask threshold and final mask threshold); as shown in Table 6, pixel-level metrics exhibit sensitivity to these thresholds depending on defect size and category morphology.

strengths: Practical and timely problem setting: Zero-shot anomaly generation (ZSAG) avoids the requirement of real defective samples and fine-tuning, which is well-suited for industrial inspection scenarios characterized by extreme defect scarcity.

Well-structured and coherent framework: The integration of delta-denoising attribution for mask discovery, normal-reference guided initialization, mask-guided latent inpainting, and spatial cross-attention biasing forms an effective pipeline for training-free anomaly synthesis.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The authors conduct extensive comparisons across MVTec AD and VisA against representative ZSAG (AnomalyAny, AnoStyler) and FSAG baselines, demonstrating solid improvements in downstream detection metrics (AUC and AP at both image and pixel levels).

Model-agnostic extensibility: The framework demonstrates successful application across different diffusion backbones, showing notable performance improvements when switching from Stable Diffusion v1.5 to FLUX.1-dev without requiring architecture-specific modifications.

Thorough supplementary ablations and discussions: The paper provides informative analyses regarding threshold sensitivity, SAM dependency, computational efficiency (showing favorable runtime/memory compared to AnomalyAny), and thoughtful reflections on existing ZSAG evaluation metrics in Appendix D.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: The core components heavily draw upon existing diffusion-based editing paradigms—specifically, mask extraction via contrastive prompt denoising (conceptually very similar to DiffEdit), partial noise initialization (SDEdit), and attention biasing/injection (similar to Prompt-to-Prompt and Attend-and-Excite). The synthesis and application to anomaly generation are effective, but the underlying mechanisms are mostly adaptations of established image editing techniques.

Reliance on external priors (SAM): The early-stage spatial attention biasing relies on a foreground mask extracted using SAM. Although the ablation in Appendix C.2 shows only moderate degradation without SAM (pixel AUROC drops from 84.9% to 82.1%), the default pipeline remains dependent on an external segmentation foundation model.

Heuristic prompt engineering: The token-level refinement relies on auxiliary description prompts (e.g., 'some large and deep {anomaly type}'), which reintroduces manual text-tuning and prompt heuristics. A systematic sensitivity analysis of generation quality across varying phrasing or vocabulary choices is lacking.

Uneven downstream performance on challenging categories: Performance remains suboptimal on several categories exhibiting complex structures or subtle defects (e.g., capsule image AUROC is 54.9% with SD1.5, screw pixel AP is below 5%, and macaroni2 yields poor detection results), highlighting fundamental difficulties of diffusion models in capturing high-precision industrial anomalies without in-domain supervision.

Downstream validation scope: While training a U-Net on synthesized samples adheres to the protocol in AnomalyAny, the paper does not explore how synthesized samples benefit or integrate with established zero-shot/few-shot detection models (e.g., WinCLIP or AnomalyCLIP) or compare against standard memory-based baselines.
